items.title: AI Isn’t a Feature You Switch On. It’s a Capability You Build. - Planview Blog
items.snippet:
## A feature is switched on. A capability is built.

A feature is something you ...
items.raw_snippet:
## A feature is switched on. A capability is built.

A feature is something you turn on. Flip the switch, and it works or it doesn’t.

A capability is different. You have to work to enable it. Think of AI as a new hire, not a new button.

Nobody expects a new hire to know your acronyms, your reporting quirks, or which numbers leadership trusts on their first morning. You onboard them, and they get more useful every week. [...] Weeks later, the same organization described the AI as the foundation everything else in their platform rests on.

It was the same product. What changed was what they had built around it.

The gap between the first day and a few weeks later is where AI value is won or lost. If you judge AI by what it does on day one, you will always be early to buy and late to benefit.

Coming on Oct. 22: Join the 15-minute microwebinar, “Don’t Judge AI by What it Does on Day 1” [...] Buyers were trained to expect features. Nearly every AI tool shipped as a chat box, and a chat box looks finished. An empty text field implies you can ask anything and get the answer. So organizations switch it on and hope.

That hope has a cost. A weak first answer is hard to overcome. People try the AI, get a poor result, and don’t feel like using it again. That is what judging on day one looks like.

## What you build around AI matters

items.title: How to Hire AI Engineers: A Startup Hiring Guide
items.snippet: When you hire AI developers, proof of real work beats a fancy resume. Check thes...
items.raw_snippet:
When you hire AI developers, proof of real work beats a fancy resume. Check these places:

 Open-source projects: Look for people who contribute to AI tools and libraries.
 Technical communities: Forums and data science groups show how people think and solve problems.
 Talks and papers: These show who can explain hard ideas in plain words.
 Your own network: A trusted engineer or founder often knows who gets things shipped.

### Write Outreach People Answer [...] A fair salary: It doesn’t need to be the highest, but it must be believable for the market.
 Clear equity talk: Explain how it works in plain words. Good candidates will ask.
 Real ownership: “You will lead our AI search feature” beats “you will help with AI projects.”
 Direct access: Time with founders and fast decisions matter to many engineers.

### Be Honest in the Final Talks

Most offers fail before they are sent. The candidate still has doubts about the plan, the budget, or the data. [...] 1. Portfolio review: Ask the candidate to walk you through something they shipped.
2. Problem framing: Give a real product problem and see how they think.
3. Work sample: Assign a small task, then talk through every choice.
4. Team chat: Make sure they can work well with product and design people.

### Ask Questions That Reveal Real Experience

In the portfolio review, ask what broke first in production. Ask how they checked quality before launch. Ask what they would change today.
